title: Reading Hieratic
short: Egyptologists read hieratic by transcribing it, sign by sign, into hieroglyphs, then transliterating.
trouble: Students think hieratic is a separate language. It is the same language in a faster hand.

blocks.html: Since hieratic has no standard font and every scribe's hand differs, Egyptologists do not usually print it. Instead they transcribe it: they write out each hieratic sign as the hieroglyph it stands for. Then they read the hieroglyphs as they would any inscription.

Reading hieratic takes three steps: transcribe each hieratic sign into its hieroglyph (using a table of sign forms by date, such as Georg Möller's), transliterate the hieroglyphs into the Egyptological alphabet, and translate. Editions often print the hieroglyphic transcription beside a photograph of the papyrus.

Transcription separates two jobs. The first, identifying each cursive sign, needs a specialist's eye and a palaeography table, and it is where most uncertainty lies, so it is shown openly in the edition. The second, reading the hieroglyphs, is the same as for any carved text. A reader who doubts a transcription can check the photograph, sign by sign.

items: Transcribe: hieratic sign → hieroglyph (with its Gardiner code). Doubtful signs are marked.
Transliterate: hieroglyphs → the consonants, as in nfr.

blocks.cap: A transcribed word: the heart-and-windpipe sign with f and r as phonetic complements, read nfr, "good, beautiful".

blocks.title: From transcription to meaning
blocks.q: A papyrus has been transcribed into the signs for the house plan and a stroke. Read it.
steps: The house plan (O1) with a stroke is a word sign: it means what it shows.

blocks.title: Where the doubt lies
blocks.q: An edition marks one hieroglyph in its transcription with a question mark. What does that tell you?
steps: The editor was not sure which hieroglyph the cursive sign stands for: hieratic forms of some signs look alike.
The reading of that word depends on the choice, so it is less certain than the rest.
Check the photograph and a palaeography table before relying on it.
blocks.a: The identification of that hieratic sign is uncertain.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: sḏm "hear": once transcribed, a hieratic word is read like any hieroglyphic one.

blocks.html: Hieratic hands changed over time and from place to place. A Middle Kingdom literary papyrus and a Ramesside account can look very different, so palaeography tables arrange each sign's forms by date and by manuscript. Experienced readers learn to date a papyrus roughly from its handwriting alone, much as a historian can tell an 18th-century letter from a modern one.

blocks.name: eg-scripts
blocks.cap: One word, sḏm "hear", through the scripts: transcription brings a hieratic word back to this hieroglyphic form.

blocks.html: Thinking hieratic is a separate language. It is the same language in a faster hand. Transcription changes the script, not the words.
